questiontext.text:
A town has {@areastxt@}, joined by {@nE@} bridges as in the table.

[[foreach row="blist"]][[/foreach]]
BridgeJoins
{@row[1]@}{@row[2]@} and {@row[3]@}

Suppose that a route crosses every bridge exactly once, and write it as a list of areas, as Euler did.

  1. How many letters does the list have?

    [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

  2. Euler's rule says how many times each area must appear in the list. What is the total of these numbers, over all the areas?

    [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

  3. Does Euler's counting prove that there is no such route?

    [[input:ans3]] [[validation:ans3]] [[feedback:prt3]]

generalfeedback.text:
A route that crosses {@nE@} bridges is a list of {@nL@} letters: the starting area, and one more letter for each bridge crossed.

By Euler's rule, an area with an odd number \(d\) of bridges appears \(\dfrac{d + 1}{2}\) times in the list. Here {@perarea@}. So the list needs {@sumtxt@} = {@tot@} letters in all.

[[if test='contra']]But the list has only {@nL@} letters. This is a contradiction, so no route crosses every bridge exactly once.[[else]]The list has {@nL@} letters too, so the counts agree and the argument gives no contradiction. In fact there is such a route: {@routetxt@}. Euler's argument proves that a route is impossible only when the counts are too big for the list.[[/if]]

questiondescription.text: This question is based on Example 8.8 (pp. 42-44) in Section 8 of Bokhove, C., Thoma, A., Gammack, D., Yu, L. H. S., Roberts, S. and Downey, F., Thinking about Proof, 1st edition, University of Southampton, 2022: Euler's counting is applied to other arrangements of land and bridges.

truefeedback.text: Yes: the starting area, then one more letter for each of the {@nE@} bridges.
A route over one bridge has two letters: where it starts and where it ends. Each bridge adds one letter to the starting one.

falsefeedback.text: Count the starting area, then one more letter for each bridge crossed.

node.description: Diagnostic: bridges counted at both ends

truefeedback.text: That counts bridges, not appearances. An area appears once for each visit, and a visit usually uses two of its bridges, one in and one out.
Euler's rule is to add one before halving: an area with \(d\) bridges, \(d\) odd, appears \(\dfrac{d + 1}{2}\) times.

falsefeedback.text: For each area, take its number of bridges \(d\) and work out \(\dfrac{d + 1}{2}\). Then add these up.

node.description: Conclusion. Binary choice: the false branch carries the explanation, so this PRT has no separate diagnostic

truefeedback.text: [[if test='contra']]Yes. The areas need more letters than the list has. That is a contradiction, so no such route exists.[[else]]Right: the two counts agree, so the argument gives no contradiction. In fact a route does exist here: try to find one.[[/if]]

falsefeedback.text: Compare the two counts from parts (a) and (b). [[if test='contra']]If the areas need more letters than the list has, the supposed route cannot exist: that is a contradiction.[[else]]Euler's counting proves that no route exists only when the areas need more letters than the list has. When the counts agree there is no contradiction, and here a route does exist.[[/if]]
